#891. Spain in pain as historic run ends but De la Fuente feels best is yet to come

While the head coach, players and Spanish press were magnanimous in defeat, there was pride mixed in with disappointment – and confidence the future is still bright

“With every game, defeat gets closer,” Luis de la Fuente had said and on Sunday night it finally came. Spain had lost only one competitive game since Scotland in March 2023 back when the coach hadn’t won anything and didn’t look like he ever would – and that solitary loss was on penalties in the 2025 Nations League final. Statistically, they said, penalties don’t count, so while Portugal lifted the trophy that night, the team that won the European Championship and World Cup in the summers either side also claimed a Fifa record of 44 official games unbeaten. And then England turned up at the Metropolitano.

A night that started with Iker Casillas, Fernando Torres and Fernando Llorente handing the World Cup to Unai Simón ended with Spain trying to overhaul a shock 3-0 deficit. Against 10 men and led by a superb Lamine Yamal, Spain made De la Fuente think for a while that they would too, but it wasn’t to be.

Aymeric Laporte had almost levelled it in the 91st minute, denied by James Trafford. “I thought it was in, but that’s football,” the defender said, and in football some days you lose, especially against opponents such as these. “This could have been the World Cup final,” the coach said.

Had it been, who knows, this might have been different. From a Spanish perspective, better to lose now, with both teams already through to the Nations League quarter‑finals, than somewhere else: better than Berlin, June 2024, that’s for sure. There might even have been some value in it, the coach welcoming a glimpse of “reality” and claiming that everything he took from the defeat was positive. Thomas Tuchel had said Spain can look “invincible” but sometimes it helps to be reminded you’re not. Which isn’t to say they wanted it to happen now, still less that they didn’t care. “It’s a pity,” Mikel Oyarzabal said. “It hurts,” Simón admitted. “But we knew at some point it could happen.”

Not that the analysis ends there. Before the game Simón had lifted the trophy in the absence of Rodri, who was replaced by Martín Zubimendi. And although De la Fuente likes to say that Zubimendi is the second-best central midfielder in the world after the captain, although Zubimendi was on the pitch when they won the European Championship and the World Cup, he has not started a Premier League game for Arsenal and faced Declan Rice, who has started 10. “Sometimes it’s not easy to come to the national team when you’re not playing many minutes,” Zubimendi had accepted after a narrow win against Czechia three days earlier. There was also a start for Mikel Merino too, often the supersub. And not for Pedri.

Asked about Pedri’s absence, De la Fuente shot back: “Fabián’s not a bad player either, is he?” The past two tournaments have ended with Pedri losing out – to Dani Olmo at No 10 at Euro 2024 and to Fabián Ruiz in central midfield at the World Cup. They have also ended with Spain winning the titles, the decision justified; the Barcelona midfielder has begun only two of the past nine matches for Spain, and they have won eight. Yet the continued absence of a midfielder who may be the most talented in the team is disconcerting, maybe even feels like a defeat in itself. At the Metropolitano it was in midfield, unusually, where Spain did not take control and he helped change the game when introduced.

De la Fuente also admitted that Spain had been struggling from dead balls – in fact that was part of the reason to include Marc Pubill and Merino. That has been a constant since the World Cup, Simón said, and it showed on the second goal. Olmo was absent. It was not easy to live with the intensity England imposed. And Laporte called it a “peculiar” week: he had missed Prague with a virus that others had feared catching too. There had also been the debate about Lamine Yamal before the game, and none whatsoever about him after it.

Yet more than the analysis, much of which will have morphed by March when the national team meet up again, there was a certain acceptance. Appreciation too, for Spain and for their opponents. “After three years and 44 games unbeaten, it would be a bit strange to say: ‘This has to change.’ I don’t feel that way at all,” De la Fuente said, and everyone agreed.

What happened? England happened. “The second-best team in the world, comparable to us,” as Simón called them. Oyarzabal talked about how Tuchel’s team had gone man to man all over the pitch, a team of “clear ideas”. Laporte spoke of how deeply they had studied Spain. “They overran us in the first 30 minutes, they were superior throughout most of the game … and we still nearly turned it around,” De la Fuente said.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

No excuses: England were just better, “a formidable opponent: voracious, ambitious, scorching”, in El País’s words. “If you’re going to lose your run, better to do it against an imposing opponent like England,” said Marca. Spain were “obliged to recognise they had a stupendous rival before them, defeat is not unjust”, El Mundo wrote.

“This can happen against England,” Simón said. It was just that they had “forgotten what defeat tastes like”, De la Fuente admitted, and while that wasn’t nice it was also something of which to be proud.

“This serves to underline what we have done,” he repeated over and over and over again; it served to value a record-breaking run, the trophies won en route and what lies ahead.

It was time to build towards another record but that didn’t mean beginning again, it meant carrying on. “The best is yet to come,” De la Fuente said. “This shows how hard it is to get here. As they say: ‘Let’s see you beat that.’”

At the end of the match, De la Fuente lined up alongside his staff and applauded his players off the pitch, a guard of honour for the men who had made history. “In the dressing room they were sad,” he said. “But I told them: ‘Gentlemen, do you know what you’ve done? Do you know where we are? This is historic. Let’s see if anyone ever matches this. Maybe they will … or maybe they won’t.’”

#890. Van Gerwen: I need my A-game to beat Wade at Grand Slam

Michael van Gerwen on his second-round opponent: "James Wade is playing some fantastic darts; he's probably in some of the best form of his life"; pair's meeting a rematch of 2016 final which MVG won; watch the Grand Slam of Darts on Sky Sports Main Event at 7pm, Thursday

Michael van Gerwen believes James Wade is "in some of the best form of his life" and says he'll need to bring his "A-game" in order to win their second-round meeting at the Grand Slam of Darts.

Their clash on Thursday night - live on Sky Sports+ and Main Event from 7pm - is a rematch of the 2016 final, in which Van Gerwen claimed the second of his three consecutive titles.

But it's Wade, a three-time runner-up at the event, who is the form player of the pair leading into the last 16 matchup, having dropped only one leg across his two group-stage wins.

Van Gerwen, contrastingly, saw both his wins over Henry Coates and Jeffrey de Graaf come down to last-leg deciders. He averaged 100 against Coates, but that dropped to 90 against De Graaf, a match in which he missed seven match darts.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"It wasn't a good game at all," Van Gerwen, seeded 10th at the tournament, told Sky Sports after his victory over De Graaf.

"Sometimes you're not doing what you want to do. That's frustrating, because I know I'm capable of doing a lot more.

"What can I say? I am through to the next round - that's all history now - and it's onto the next one."

The former world No 1 added: "James Wade is playing some fantastic darts, you can't deny that. He's probably in some of the best form of his life.

"I need to make sure I play my A-game if I'm going to beat him - simple as that."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Wade has been in sensational form across 2026, making it to the final of the UK Open, winning the Australian Masters, Flanders Darts Trophy, and the opening Players Championship event back in February.

He knows that, with his form at the minute, he has the game to beat anyone, especially if the contest is a bit of a grudge match.

"I think I am way better than the top 10 but I have had to bumble along," said the seventh seed, who has averaged over 100 in both of his Grand Slam group stage wins against Cam Crabtree (5-1) and Ricky Evans (5-0).

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I think if I was probably a little bit more consistent, I would be better than I am.

"But talk is cheap and all that rubbish. I think I am good enough to beat anyone at the moment, because I like a scrap and no darts player wants to have a scrap.

"Most of them just want to have a little gallivant along the meadows and stuff like that, but I am quite happy to take them to a place where most of the younger players don't want to go and that is when I win games."

Luke Humphries, the 2023 Grand Slam champion, is also in action on Thursday night, against Tom Sykes, while Gian van Veen faces Martin Schindler and Nathan Aspinall takes on Gabriel Clemens.

"There has been so much made of James Wade's form. He is playing great.

"I don't really get Michael van Gerwen at the moment. A couple of weeks ago he was playing in a Pro Tour event and was averaging 114, 115. He also looked great in his opening group game here, but then looked really edgy in his second.

"Having said that, normally with Michael, the longer the format the less edgy he looks. I'm not saying he'll beat James, but I don't buy into this narrative that Michael is off. He's just not as consistent as he used to be.

"He portrays a lack of confidence at times with what he says, which I don't like.

"I believe he is capable of growing into a game. His confidence grows after a couple of decent legs.

"But if James Wade gets on top of him, I don't like Van Gerwen's chances from there."

#889. Ronaldo, Maradona, Baggio - what happened to the World XI?

Soren Colding wasn't expecting the call. "The Laudrup brothers, Peter Schmeichel, there might have been some cancellations," he jokes.

Eventually, the Danish FA turned to a Brondby defender who had played a handful of times for the national team.

The assignment? He would be expected to mark Ronaldo and Gabriel Batistuta as part of a Europe XI against the Rest of the World at Marseille's Velodrome.

It was December 1997, and Colding's team-mates would include defenders Fernando Hierro and Alessandro Costacurta, a midfield duo of Zinedine Zidane and Paul Ince, and Patrick Kluivert and Alen Boksic up top.

This was a star-sprinkled cast - one player from each of the competing nations at the following summer's World Cup joining forces before the draw took place.

"Of course, when you see those names, it was just more or less a dream come true," explains the Dane.

Colding was flown to France and chauffeured to the hotel. His driver offered to hang around in case the full-back fancied an impromptu shopping trip. There was no need. Instead, he discovered a bag of Fifa goodies in his room.

"There was the biggest Adidas bag I have ever seen in my life," he smiles. "I found a training suit and went down to lunch.

"Then I saw all the other guys on round tables - they were sitting with their agents, their wives, their family, their friends in normal [clothes]. Then the Danish guy turned in. Nobody knows who he is, in his Adidas training suit!"

Colding struck up a friendship with South Africa defender David Nyathi and the pair were whisked off to a 45-minute training session that afternoon. Not all the big names took part, but one Argentine offered a taste of what was to come.

"Batistuta was there and just to see him and his moves, you thought, 'Okay, it's gonna be a nice evening tomorrow'," remembers Colding, who also got to link up with European boss Franz Beckenbauer.

"He was pretty cool. He was saying, 'what is your position? Defender? OK, can you play left defender?' No problem - I'll play wherever you place me!"

Ronaldo scored twice and assisted three more goals as Rest of the World beat their Europe counterparts 5-2 in Marseille

Come game day, 38,000 fans packed in to see peak Ronaldo. Months earlier, Il Fenomeno completed a world-record move to Inter Milan on the back of 47 goals in 49 games in one sensational season at Barcelona.

The 21-year-old was the most exciting player on the planet.

"It was crazy, actually," recalls Colding, who previously faced the forward when Denmark's under-21s played Brazil in Florianopolis before the 1996 Olympics.

"That was almost the same team as they played with at the World Cup in '98. So we lost 5-1. Just to see his speed and how he played - I played against Roberto Carlos in that game as well - that was just another level. I thought, 'what is going on here?'

"When I saw him there again, it was just to see what is actually reachable for a football player, because that was next level tremendous. His speed and his touch are unbelievable, and also his power.

"And still, just a small, shy guy. You know, he just wants to play football, and all these people are around him protecting him. Just to see when a star like him joins an event like that, how many people around him, agents and followers, how should you navigate all that?"

Ronaldo, captaining Carlos Alberto Parreira's side, was at his blistering best, scoring twice and setting up the other three as Rest of the World won 5-2 - Batistuta also netted twice, before Zidane responded.

"You start thinking what if you injured some of them," explains Colding. "You are a defender, you don't want goals against you, so you have to fight - that's how I am.

"How hard should you go to them? Should you just let them go? No. I would not just let them run and score. I tried to do my best, that was probably not good enough!"

1987: Maradona stars in FA Centenary all-star game

This wasn't the first outing for a World XI, in fact such Fifa exhibition matches had been taking place since England hosted an all-star side in front of a reported 100,000 fans at Wembley in 1963 to celebrate the Football Association's centenary.

They became a semi-regular occurrence as testimonials or charity fixtures, with huge names appearing across eras from Eusebio and Zico to Roberto Baggio.

But the biggest coup was arguably luring Diego Maradona to Wembley a year after winning the World Cup with Argentina and scoring his 'Hand of God' goal against England.

Jon Smith, who represented the Napoli star, explains in his book 'The Deal' how Maradona was offered around Â£250,000 and flown from Naples on a private jet to take part in an anniversary game against the Football League.

"In fairness, he wanted to shake hands with the team and say 'sorry if I offended you'," Smith tells BBC Sport. "He genuinely believed his talent was God-given.

"He was sort of two people. He was lovely, Diego, when you were with him. When he crossed the white line he was Maradona. So the Hand of God was an expression of 'I am God's footballing representative', if you like.

"It was madness, because you can imagine how the media were all over it. It was a bit special."

Napoli and Argentina welcomed the opportunity for Maradona to generate some good PR in England, helped by Bobby Robson's Football League side winning 3-0 - Bryan Robson netting twice and Norman Whiteside grabbing the other.

"I remember introducing him to Bobby Robson," adds Smith. "He put his hand out, and Bobby said 'I'm not shaking that hand!', which I thought was lovely - he did shake the other hand!"

A Ronaldinho XI beat their Shevchenko counterparts 6-3 in February 2005 - Ronaldinho, Samuel Eto'o, Alessandro Del Piero and Gianfranco Zola were all on the scoresheet

One of the final games saw a Ronaldinho XI take on a Shevchenko XI at Nou Camp in February 2005 to raise funds for victims of the 2004 tsunami.

Andriy Shevchenko's stacked squad included Zidane, David Beckham, Alessandro Del Piero, Thierry Henry, Raul, Paolo Maldini and Steven Gerrard.

Ronaldinho could call on Ronaldo, Kaka, Cafu, Adriano, Javier Zanetti, Didier Drogba and Samuel Eto'o, though it was Southampton's Henri Camara who scored twice in a 6-3 win for the Brazilian's team.

But things have moved on, and it is hard to imagine clubs releasing their star players for such an exhibition nowadays.

"The whole world of football has changed," says Smith. "You used to have testimonial games and testimonial years because players got paid okay but by the same token weren't earning Â£100k a week.

"It wouldn't happen now because the business of football is so much bigger, you can't risk the players - if they get injured playing for their country, that annoys everybody.

"But beyond that they are owned by big corporations and in some cases countries, so you just wouldn't allow your player to go out and do that."

Colding went on to play 27 times for Denmark, featuring at the 1998 World Cup and Euro 2000, but retains fond memories of representing the Europe XI.

"Now, to come up with the idea to make a game like this, in combination with the draw, I think everyone will say you are crazy," explains Colding.

"But at that time it was perfectly planned and a fantastic event to be a part of. As players, we have a tremendous relationship between each other.

"It shows all the spectators you can be enemies on the field, but you can actually be friends and gather together in this kind of event.

"That for me sends a signal to all that we are a community in football and we can actually make great things together that not only is a question of money."

In fact, he still has his Europe shirt - a reminder of coming up against Ronaldo and Batistuta and being a team-mate of Zidane almost 30 years ago.

"It doesn't smell very good, actually," laughs Colding. "Sometimes, when I go in the garage with my kids and tell them about it and what actually happened, I see in their eyes, they don't really believe that I was a part of that game.

"That was not about money - we didn't get anything to join - it was just because you represent your country, so it was a great experience, it's also about having fun.

"You know, as small kids, you don't start by saying, 'I want to earn 20 million'. No, you start because it's fun to play football."

Soren Colding still has the shirt he wore for the Europe XI almost 30 years ago

#888. Echoes of Azteca but not like Argentina: fearless England start afresh in Madrid

‘We will not go back on this way of playing,’ says Thomas Tuchel after he delivered response to World Cup critics

Thomas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead. He finished with three centre-backs on the pitch. His team could not get out of their half in the final part of the game. So close your eyes and imagine an alternate universe in which James Trafford did not make his stunning double save in stoppage time on Sunday and England had drawn 3-3 with Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium rather than won 3-2. The reaction would not have been kind because Tuchel has been here before.

The head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer. “It was Mexico reloaded,” he said, with a nod towards the 3-2 last-16 win at the Azteca Stadium and it fitted like a glove – down to the detail of Jarell Quansah and red cards.

Against Mexico, the defender was sent off for a late tackle in the 54th minute with England 2-1 up. Against Spain, he contributed to Elliot Anderson being sent off in the 63rd minute with England 3-0 up. Quansah had his pocket picked by Lamine Yamal and Anderson’s attempt to chase back and rectify the situation ended with him fouling the winger.

It was not only a red card but a penalty; the prompt for Spain to launch a furious and hitherto unadvertised fightback. It had the stand that housed the press box shaking. Structural integrity was very much a theme.

As in Mexico, Tuchel made defensive changes. This time, it was Myles Lewis-Skelly for Harry Kane; Djed Spence for Anthony Gordon. Tuchel also withdrew Jude Bellingham, who went off shaking his head. It was easy to understand his frustration. He was excellent. Tuchel had removed his two prime attackers. He also put Dan Burn on towards the end, albeit this time not as part of a back five. England stayed in a 4-4-1 formation, with Quansah moving from central defence to right-back. As in Mexico, the 10-man low block resisted.

As much as Tuchel disagreed, this felt like Argentina reloaded as well. “No, not at all,” he said, when the World Cup semi-final defeat was raised. “Because of one man down. We would not have been in this situation if it was 11 against 11.”

The parallels, nevertheless, were there. Tuchel made defensive substitutions at 1-0 up against Argentina; it was a back five on that occasion. As against Spain, his team could not get out and they faced a flurry of chances. There were other factors in play at the World Cup, chief among them the high levels of fatigue within the squad. England could not hold out, conceding two late goals to exit and bring down a wave of criticism on Tuchel.

The score is the ultimate takeaway. It can skew analysis. Had Trafford not got back up after parrying a shot from the Spain substitute Fermín López to brilliantly repel Aymeric Laporte’s follow‑up, England would have gone from enjoying a fabulous result to stewing over an opportunity missed. The stakes were nowhere near as high as at the World Cup, but they would have gone from finishing top of their Nations League group to advancing into the quarter-finals as an unseeded second-place team.

In terms of Tuchel’s approach to the closing stages of a big game, what changed?

The truth for England lay in the opening 63 minutes. This was where the evidence of a decisive shift could be found, the reasons for the swell of optimism. England have never played better under Tuchel – and this was against the team to beat; the world and European champions. On their turf.

Spain were without the injured Rodri and Dani Olmo, and Luis de la Fuente strangely decided to use Pedri only as a substitute, but their lineup still shimmered with menace; Lamine Yamal was frightening. Yet before their penalty, converted by Mikel Oyarzabal, they did not have a shot on target. Or a real chance.

What stood out from the first whistle was England’s front‑foot intent; the bravery on the ball. They believed they would win and there was a fearlessness about them. They made forward moves on the half turn. There was a slickness about their combinations.

Spain have never suffered like this under De la Fuente and it was everything Tuchel had dreamed of when he started to plot a new version of his team after the World Cup; a more fluid game model, a response to the Argentina defeat.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Tuchel loved England’s buildup play, which included some of Trafford’s passing. He loved the high press; the aggression in the duels; the threat on set pieces. He said he loved the low-block defending too. Ben White was excellent at right-back and there was a coming-of-age performance from Lewis Hall at left-back, but it felt wrong to single out individuals.

“We didn’t stop and I think we are ready to go [like this] for 90 minutes,” Tuchel said. “It was a complete performance and we will not look back now. Go forward and stay hungry. We will not go back on this way of playing that we find ourselves since the World Cup.”

Ezri Konsa, who headed in the second goal from a Declan Rice corner, said England “would have scored two more” if they had kept 11 men on the pitch. “You saw until the red card how much quality we had,” he said.

“We dominated the game. The instruction was to keep going at them. Don’t stop. To keep our foot on the pedal. Argentina was different; different circumstances.”

Tuchel was asked about the journey from the heartbreak of Argentina to this point; the end of a stirring Nations League group campaign, including the 7-0 win against Croatia in Rijeka. It has not all been super exciting; the 2-1 Wembley win against Croatia last Thursday, for example, was a grind. Was he always confident of a successful reboot?

“It took me a while to digest [the World Cup] and see the way forward,” he said. “How we can help and adjust and improve? We had reviews and so on but the clarity came in the first Nations League camp [in September and October] with the players.

“The first week was not so easy. Some players were still upset from the World Cup. Some were new in the team. Some had digested it, some had not. But it was important to have this process together and everyone committed to wanting to improve in certain aspects of the game.

“We had the energy right to take the next steps and from there we went. Full credit to the players, how they buy in. It’s amazing that it came together like this now.”

#887. Price hopes undisputed history could lead her to Shields showdown

Olympic gold medallist Lauren Price wants to test herself against Claressa Shields, Chantelle Cameron and Mikaela Mayer; Price will become Wales' first undisputed world champion in the four-belt era if she beats Michaela Kotaskova and hopes victory can lead to American star Shields

Sports Journalist @johndennen

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Lauren Price believes becoming an undisputed champion could lead her to a showdown with American star Claressa Shields.

Price faced off with Shields after her last fight but no agreement has been reached for them to box.

Shields has been an undisputed champion in multiple divisions and has returned to middleweight after a period as the undisputed heavyweight champion.

Price, like Shields, won the Olympic gold medal at middleweight. She's unbeaten as a professional too. On Friday Price looks to add the now vacant WBO welterweight title to the WBA, WBC and IBF belts she already holds when she fights Michaela Kotaskova.

If she wins she will become Wales' first undisputed champion in the four-belt era.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"It hasn't sunk in yet," Price told Sky Sports. "When I turned over, that's the dream to become undisputed. I can honestly say if I achieve that on Friday then I've ticked every accolade in boxing.

"Regardless of the belts on the line, you step through the ropes and it's another fight. I just let the boxing do the talking and make sure I get that win and I win in style."

If Price does go undisputed at welterweight, moving up through divisions will be the natural next step. Shields remains a target though that fight is yet to come to fruition.

"It has to make sense on both ends," Price said. "I'm giving away weight, fine. But it was in her back garden, I wanted to come back to Wales as well.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

On December 24 Chantelle Cameron and Mikaela Mayer, who vacated the WBO welterweight title, will rematch for the WBA, WBC and WBO super-welter championships. Price has an eye on fighting the winner.

"They're both great. But I believe Chantelle will win that fight again and that's a great fight for British boxing, I'm 100 percent up for it," Price said.

"I think right now obviously myself, Cameron, Mayer's in there [the pound-for-pound list] and obviously Shields. For me we're the big names and that's what I want, I want the big fights."

#886. FA wants to host Nations League finals in England

England finished top of their Nations League group

England could host the Nations League finals this season after Football Association officials registered their interest.

The semi-final and finals of the competition, due to take place in June, are held in one country.

As well as England, it is understood that Spain and France have also contacted Uefa to register their interest in hosting the final four games, including the bronze medal match, which will run between 9-13 June.

The FA, it is understood, is still discussing potential venues with some doubt over whether Wembley would be available. The only publicly announced Wembley events in June are two concerts by singer Sam Fender, although these are for after the Nations League.

Since the tournament began in 2019, England have never held the finals, with Portugal, Italy, Netherlands and Germany the hosts to date.

Generally, only nations who reach the last four of the Nations League are considered to host the latter stages.

Thomas Tuchel's team will be seeded in Friday's draw for the quarter-finals following their euphoric 3-2 victory over Spain in Madrid, which secured top place in the group.

They could face Belgium, Netherlands, Denmark or Norway in March in the next round before June's finals.

If the FA's bid is successful, it will provide the governing body with an opportunity to host a mini-tournament before Euro 2028, which will be held in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

#885. Germany slips in climate protection rankings as other countries make gains

Record renewable energy growth is driving climate progress in some countries, but Germany and many major emitters are falling behind.

Germany has slipped down the climate action ranking for the third consecutive year, with the former green leader now being outperformed by Brazil, Colombia and Romania.

In its worst performance since 2019, the country fell to place 25 and received a "medium" rating overall on the yearly Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI), which assesses efforts to curb global warming in 64 countries plus the European Union.

Still, "a number of countries have been making good progress for years," said Jan Burck, CCPI lead author, in a statement. Denmark is leading the way across all four categories assessed — energy use, greenhouse gas emissions, renewable energy and national climate policy. A total of 15 states, including Lithuania, Chile, and Morocco, received an overall "high" rating, which is two more than last year.

The European Union also moved up a spot, while Hungary jumped 21 places after the ousting of former prime minister Viktor Orban's government, which had repeatedly vetoed EU climate plans, dismissing them as a "utopian fantasy."

The top three positions on the CCPI remained vacant again this year, as no country has yet done enough to meet global climate goals aimed at preventing worsening weather extremes and climate damage.

"We are seeing a striking contrast," said Burck. "Progress on climate action is often slow and in some countries, such as the United States, things are even moving backwards. But technologically and economically there is enormous momentum."

That momentum is apparent in record solar energy growth. Last year 75% of global electricity demand growth was met by the green energy source, according to energy think tank Ember's latest global electricity review. Investment in clean energy has also outpaced that in fossil fuels for multiple years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The rapid expansion of renewable technology, as well as the Iran War and a reduction in deforestation are behind a projected slight fall in emissions for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the CCPI.

"Governments have to act now to turn the momentum into sustained emissions reductions," said CCPI co-author Niklas Höhne of the NewClimate Institute, which compiles the report with environmental NGO Germanwatch.

Burck attributed Germany's worst ever performance in the category of national climate policy to current policies being pursued by Germany's economy minister Katherina Reiche.

"Measures that primarily aim to increase the use of natural gas, threaten to undermine progress in the energy transition and risk significantly worsening the conditions for renewable energy and electrification for many years to come," said Burck.

A European Commission report published on November 9 on the sidelines of the UN COP31 climate summit in Turkey said Germany was one of nine EU countries set to miss 2030 emissions reductions targets.

Germany is not alone in its disappointing ranking. The other G20 countries — the world's leading industrialized and emerging economies, responsible for around 80% of global CO2 emissions — also perform poorly.

The only exception among them is the United Kingdom, which ranks seventh and received a high rating, performing well in greenhouse gas emissions, energy use and climate policy. However, study authors rated it low for renewable energy expansion.

The G20's oil- and gas-producing countries occupy some of the lowest positions on the climate action table. The United States, which is the world's second largest emitter, languishes alongside Russia, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Canada around the bottom of the league, with an overall rating of "very low."

The hosts of this year's COP31, also received a "low" overall score. Australia, a major coal exporter with some of the world's highest per-capita emissions, ranks 54th, while Turkey, which is also heavily dependent on fossil fuels, comes in 53rd.

China is the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases and ranks 56th in the CCPI, receiving an overall rating of "very low." Its main weaknesses include its now high per-capita emissions and substantial energy consumption.

However, among the G20, China leads the way in renewable energy expansion. The country, which is five years ahead of schedule in reaching its goal of adding 1,200 GW of wind and solar capacity to the grid by 2030, also produces over 80% of the world's solar panels.

Several oil-producing countries, including Kazakhstan, Saudi Arabia, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates, are also performing better than expected in the renewables category and "are significantly expanding their previously limited" capacity, said the report.

The authors said these countries have significant potential to further expand renewables.

"In the Arab states in particular, very high per-capita emissions and an above-average level of electrification coincide with a relatively low existing share of renewable energy and enormous solar potential," said co-author Natalie Pelekh in a statement. "These are, in fact, ideal conditions for more ambitious climate action."

This article was originally published in German.

#883. Thomas Frank’s to-do list: lift mood, fix defence and fire up Sarr and Mateta

Seeking redemption after failing at Spurs, newly installed Crystal Palace manager has a tough challenge ahead

Thomas Frank promised his wife, Nanna, he would take a year’s sabbatical after being sacked by Tottenham in February, but he couldn’t wait that long. Having received a reported £8m payoff from Spurs, he kept an extremely low profile in the first few months after an experience at the club that sources close to the 53‑year‑old have described as “traumatic”.

Frank broke his silence at the start of June with a statement released by the League Managers Association. It said he would cover the World Cup for the BBC (thereby going head-to-head with Ange Postecoglou, his predecessor at Spurs, who worked for ITV) before “experiencing the Tour de France”, a lifelong passion. Frank usually preferred to run to Brentford’s training ground and home matches from his home in East Sheen during a nine‑year spell as assistant and then manager, but he occasionally cycled because it helped to clear his head.

By the time the statement was released the Crystal Palace chair, Steve Parish, is understood to have sounded out Frank out over his willingness to take over from Oliver Glasner. But it confirmed his intention to keep his promise and not rush back into management. “When the time is right, I will look forward to my return as a manager, ready to embrace the job with great energy and dedication,” he said.

With Palace facing the prospect of ending a 14-season stay in the Premier League – the eighth‑longest in the division – after a dreadful start under Pierre Sage, that time has arrived. Frank left Tottenham with a win ratio of 34.2% – the worst of any permanent manager in the club’s history – but has the chance to redeem himself at a club he is said to have admired from afar.

According to the biography Thomas Frank: The Premier League Diaries, by the Danish author Kasper Steenbach, published last year, Frank attended the 2025 FA Cup final victory against Manchester City with a childhood friend from Denmark who supports Palace after arranging tickets for him. Frank is said to have been impressed by the atmosphere for which Selhurst Park has become renowned. That said, the absence of the influential supporters’ group the Holmesdale Fanatics since it disbanded at the start of the season has made it less intimidating for visiting teams.

Nonetheless, Frank is said to be itching to return to the dugout after failing at Spurs, where he inherited a squad that had just won the Europa League under Postecoglou but struggled to impose himself at a club with higher expectations. Frank’s preference to play on the counterattack with a more direct style looks a better fit at Palace, although his critics will question whether his success at Brentford was really down to the system put in place by the club’s owner, Matthew Benham, that has allowed Keith Andrews to thrive since the former set-piece coach stepped into Frank’s shoes.

There is no such framework in place at Palace, with their longevity in the Premier League mainly down to a series of shrewd managerial appointments at the right time by Parish which have ensured they have not finished lower than 15th since being promoted in 2013. Frank, who is also understood to have attracted interest from Denmark in the summer and Newcastle and Fulham in recent weeks after difficult starts for Matthias Jaissle and Álvaro Arbeloa respectively, will be expected to make an immediate impression.

For now he must make do with a squad seriously lacking in leaders after the sales of Marc Guéhi, Maxence Lacroix and Daniel Muñoz this year. Frank’s first task must be to instil some defensive discipline in a side who have conceded 24 goals in 10 league games.

His Brentford side were renowned for their organisation and prowess from set pieces, an area Palace have struggled with for several seasons. He will have to tread carefully if he intends to impose the “no dickheads” policy he borrowed from the All Blacks during his time as Brentford manager.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Sage’s attempts to impose himself on the squad by dropping the defenders Jaydee Canvot and Axel Disasi for poor performances and indiscipline respectively backfired because his team kept losing, not to mention that it angered Parish. Frank, who is believed to have been offered assurances that Palace will bring in defensive reinforcements in January, faces a delicate balancing act with a squad desperately low on morale.

The futures of Ismaïla Sarr and Jean‑Philippe Mateta could be key to Palace’s prospects of avoiding the drop. Sarr was the club’s player of the year when they won the Conference League last season but he played only 107 minutes in the Premier League under Sage owing to a groin injury. The Senegal forward’s head was turned by interest from Liverpool in the summer and Frank will have to rely on his best motivational skills to get the best out of him and Mateta, who is suspended for crucial games against Coventry and Hull after his red card against Tottenham.

The France striker tried to annul the final year of his contract after a move to Milan was scuppered by a failed medical in January and he is likely to push for a move again. But he remains popular in the dressing room and could be the talisman for Palace’s survival push if Frank can persuade him that the grass may not be greener.

#881. Football comes together across Spain to honour Jesús de Miguel: ‘We’ve seen how fragile life is’

Across La Liga and beyond this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them

In the final few minutes before stepping into the arena once more, heading out for his 199th Osasuna match on Saturday evening, the man who has scored more first division goals than anyone in their history stopped his teammates for a moment and told them what it meant to wear the shirt. “This is very important,” Ante Budimir began as the dressing room, their sanctuary, fell silent around him. “We don’t have this shirt today for the sake of it. He was not chosen, and nor are we. It could have happened to anyone, anyone. Let us go knowing that we’re grateful to be on the pitch: playing, watching, warming up, sitting on the bench, whatever it may be. Boys, we were not chosen: not us, not him. Let us go, gratefully. Without thought. We have a grand day before us.”

With that, Osasuna’s players turned left out of the room, where they were joined in the tunnel by footballers from Athletic Club, rivals from the north, and together they went out past the little shrine of Saint Fermin on to the field. They carried white lilies and all wore the same white shirts with a No 9 on the back, a black ribbon and the name of Jesús de Miguel, the Tenerife striker who died after a collision on the pitch five days earlier at the age of 30. At almost exactly the same time, 2,000km away to the west, Tenerife’s squad were walking out at the Heliodoro Rodríguez López in Santa Cruz. They did not have anyone alongside them, wore black suits not white shirts and did not have a game to play either, not this week.

Two days earlier Tenerife had been in Navahermosa, La Mancha, the tiny village their teammate’s family are from, carrying the coffin of the friend their captain called “our Demigol”. They were supposed to be in Granada on Saturday; instead, they were back on the island, in their home ground, to say goodbye and pay homage. Publicly, this time. Lilies had been laid on the pitch there too, a Tenerife shirt with them, and a stage built at one end. “We’ve seen how fragile life is,” the captain, Enric Gallego, said, offering words he said could never be enough, carrying the burden for all of them. “We think of the journeys, the wins, the losses, and hold on to those moments that seemed normal, but that now … a few days ago we shared that with you. To talk of you in the past tense is unfair. None of us are prepared to live what we’re living through.”

No one ever could be. Across Spain this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them. That, Budimir had told his teammates, was something they must think about but not think about too. The players’ union in which De Miguel had a role, a footballer there for others, had asked for the competition to stop. Respect demanded that it did, they said, requesting a judge intervene when the league did not hear them. But it had gone on. The only matches postponed were those involving Tenerife; Andorra, whose goalkeeper Jesús Owono had crashed into De Miguel; and Castellón, who he had taken to the second division, delivering them to segunda for the first time in 16 years and himself for the first time at all, aged 27.

On the eve of the game that opened this weekend’s fixtures, the Sevilla head coach, Luis García, said he thought they should wait. It was too soon, too raw, too theirs. His midfielder Giorgi Kochorashvili had missed training the day before: a former Castellón player, Kochorashvili had asked permission to go to the funeral, leaving early and returning late, his mind elsewhere. Of course he could, García had replied, “we are humans above all else”. And it was not just him. García had worked with Owono – “let’s not make two victims, we have had enough; he is in hell, for sure”, he had pleaded – and now he said: “If there’s a play that’s similar … what do I say to my goalkeeper?

“We need time,” García had said. “We need to reflect.”

Instead, they played. From Seville on Friday night to Madrid on Sunday, via stadiums everywhere. It was, some suggested, the best way to pay homage to De Miguel but no one truly knew. “We can’t ask him what he would have wanted,” José Mourinho said before Madrid went to Valencia and won 3-0, Tenerife’s flag flying at half-mast at Mestalla. He might not have wanted anything at all. “You never wanted any attention,” Gallego said, but this weekend he was on all their minds.

“Forever in our memories,” the league’s line read. At every game in the first and second divisions, the ritual was repeated. Teams came out together wearing the same white shirts bearing his name. Flowers were laid, a little uncomfortably, on the spot inside the centre circle where he had fallen and there was a minute’s silence, players and officials gathered around the wreath. As they stood before Cádiz-Oviedo, tears ran down the cheeks of the Tenerife-based referee Marta Huerta de Aza. On stadium screens, an image of De Miguel appeared. On television screens, a QR code did: a link to a crowdfunding campaign for the young family he left, set up by the former Tenerife player Fran Sol.

The games began and then, in the ninth minute or as near as the referee could manage, they paused again: the teams stopped, looking up to the screen, where a video of his best moments played out. It was not always an easy watch, and some preferred not to.

At Sevilla, where fans saw Antonio Puerta collapse on the pitch and pass away, applause still offered in the 16th minute every game, Kochorashvili stood by the bench, eyes lost somewhere his mind was not. At Espanyol, where in the 21st minute they applaud Dani Jarque, the captain who died during a pre-season tour and to whom Andrés Iniesta dedicated the winning goal at the 2010 World Cup final, Álex Calatrava and Álvaro González, teammates at Castellón and Tenerife respectively, looked about to break. In the ninth minute at the Metropolitano, the place was still rocking, the timing out of sync: Giuliano Simeone had just scored, so the referee Javier Alberola Rojas allowed a couple of minutes to pass, choosing his moment, Diego Simeone helping him impose silence on the stands when he finally stopped it. Then they started again, expected to carry on regardless.

In Pamplona, Alejandro Catena, who scored the late equaliser in a 1-1 draw with Athletic, raised an Osasuna shirt with De Miguel’s name and number on the back. Theirs was the game that felt most out of place, attention drawn from where it should have been, where it was. It would not be true to say that it did not matter, the Osasuna head coach, Jagoba Arrasate, admitting he had been carried along with it like everyone else, the calmness he thought they had found in the months out of the game soon abandoned again.

As they played, grateful for the grand day that they had before them, all the days they did, the tribute continued in Tenerife. The Heliodoro had filled early, access by every gate except eight and nine, engulfed by flowers and candles. De Miguel’s shirt lay on the turf where he had, lilies to one side, a spotlight on it. Another wreath occupied the bench. A giant shirt stretched across one end where the stage was, a lectern awaiting the speakers. A cross presided over it. Staff and players wore No 9 badges on their lapels. Supporters came in Tenerife shirts. And in the yellow shirts of rivals Las Palmas, whose president and captain Kirian, who had recovered after cancer, came. “This is the Canaries I want,” said Tenerife’s majority shareholder, Rayco García.

In the seats set up on the pitch, Tenerife’s players and De Miguel’s family sat, their eyes heavy. The archbishop, Eloy Alberto Santiago led a mass. The club’s president and majority shareholder spoke. He promised they would never allow María, De Miguel’s widow, to be alone. He also announced they would adopt Carla, his 14-month-old daughter, supporting her economically until she is 18. Gallego addressed her, football as family meaning something. “I hope one day you can look back and see who your dad was, be proud of him, not just for the footballer he was but the person: for his humility, his goodness,” he said.

Sniffing, his voice breaking, the captain paid homage to his teammate, his strike partner, his friend. The kind of person, he said, who did not seem to be there, and definitely did not demand that people notice he was, but always was. A man, he noted, so disinclined to put anyone out that when his car broke down he walked home from training rather than bother anyone for a lift. That, he insisted, might not seem like much, but it said much. “Today we don’t want to talk only of the player; we want to talk about you, Jesús, about the person that was behind the shirt,” he had begun. “Above any game, any team, what really remains is the person and the impact you leave. And you were a very special person.”

Gallego gave way to the archbishop, orations led by Tenerife staff, and as the act came to a close, difficult days ahead, the spotlight taken elsewhere, the drums began and the fans belted out a familiar tune, once more with more meaningful than ever before:

double quotation markWe have to sing with even more strength if you’re losing Even those who left us sing, from heaven This will never stop We will sing to eternity.”

Then Tenerife’s players departed. They have training on Monday and next week they play.

#879. Mauricio Pochettino asked the US to believe in his project. Did he believe in it himself?

The coach’s tenure with the USMNT brought a whiplash of highs and lows. He met some goals but also left many with the impression he never truly bought in

It did not take US men’s national team coach Mauricio Pochettino very long to take his first big swing.

He’d just taken the reins of the program after a disastrous performance at the 2024 Copa América cost his predecessor his job, with the first home World Cup in three decades looming on the horizon. The federation introduced him in New York City, on the 24th floor of a building overlooking the Hudson River. In short order, he was asked about the culture surrounding the program. In his answer, he invoked the four-time World Cup champion US women.

“We need to believe that we can win,” Pochettino said that day in September 2024. “That we can win not only a game: We can win the World Cup.”

It is the type of belief that feels almost alien to observers of the US men, the type of statement that American fans yearn to hear so badly from a coach yet also roll their eyes at. For years, fans of men’s soccer in the US have been desperate to taste glory, and for years they have developed an inferiority complex spurred along not only by results but by international perception. Even in the present day, with American players playing in Europe at the very highest level, the idea that the US could win a men’s World Cup feels borderline preposterous.

That never stopped Pochettino from espousing his belief that the US should believe they could make a miraculous run in 2026 and win the whole thing. It was a mantra he returned to frequently during his time leading the team, publicly and privately, even in the weeks leading up to the tournament. Pochettino even told Donald Trump that the US could win it all, perhaps planting the seeds for an assist turned own-goal down the line.

Belief is something that could attract even the most casual US fans, the type of newcomers whose previous experience with an American soccer coach came from Apple TV. Unfortunately for US fans, Pochettino’s actions never quite lined up with the inspirational speech.

There was the near-constant stream of rumors attaching Pochettino to clubs in England, rumors he never really went out of his way to quash even before they tied him to the Manchester United job he has now accepted. In many ways this type of thing is unavoidable and understandable: bringing on a high-profile coach and expecting peace and quiet is the footballing equivalent of dating a supermodel and expecting no one else to make an advance. Yet too often it felt as if Pochettino was the one stoking the fire; it was not uncommon to wake up in the States and find social media feeds populated with clips of the Argentinian espousing the valor of the Premier League and even floating the idea of returning someday.

This was never really shocking or unexpected and was far from offensive. Professional sports are fickle and players, coaches and administrators alike are wise to keep their options open and their bridges intact. Yet it was a bit galling to hear from someone brought in to galvanize the US’s players and fans ahead of a generational event: a home World Cup.

Pochettino also seemed sometimes frustrated by the very thing he was in part brought in to help change: American soccer’s sometimes awkward place in America itself. After losing the 2025 Gold Cup final to Mexico in Houston, he went out of his way to criticize the idea that the US would play in front of a pro-Mexico crowd on home soil, an issue that predates Pochettino by decades and may well never be solved, one even the most cursory research would’ve revealed prior to arrival. He fairly criticized the lack of stakes in Major League Soccer and suggested that US players are coddled throughout their youth development while at the same time butting heads with media who dared question the effects of a group-stage loss to Turkey at this summer’s World Cup. In reality, he faced far less pressure as the head coach of the USMNT than he would have in most any other major footballing nation.

All of it too often gave observers the feeling that Pochettino was never truly bought in. But then, there was the whiplash, which was palpable. As soon as one began to feel that way, there’d be a fresh injection of dopamine – the US’s 4-1 demolishing of Paraguay, for example, far and away their best-ever performance at a World Cup. And there was Poch, nearly in tears and belting out Country Roads, then speaking glowingly about America, American football and everything else that comes along with it. A few weeks later, they’d suffer a 4-1 drubbing at the hands of Belgium in the last 16 that will go down as among the worst-ever performances by the US at a World Cup. Certainly the most traumatic.

Athletes and coaches hate being asked about their legacies, in general. The question in and of itself sounds moribund, as if the person asked is about to ascend into the ether. Legacies, too, are tricky things – they often take years to materialize, and they’re sometimes just as quickly erased by shifting perceptions or the accomplishments of successors.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

Pochettino does not seem to be the kind of person who would mind being asked about his legacy; he actually seems more like one who would already have one in mind before departure. Yet when asked by the Guardian on Friday to define his lasting impact, he struggled to do so at first. “I am not arrogant,” Pochettino replied with a smile and a laugh. “Well, not arrogant enough. I am a little bit arrogant.”

Eventually he relented. Pochettino’s lasting impact, the coach said, was largely down to relationships, to having done things the right way, in his mind.

“The most valuable feeling that we get isn’t one victory, or that we helped in the program,” he said. “It is that relationship in the program – even when you cross the sea, you look and smile because I think you share the values that are very important in life, more important than anything else. That is our principal that we respect always.”

Pochettino has always thought in big, broad, ambitious strokes and has executed those visions over the course of his career with varying degrees of success. In the United States, he arrived with varying goals: ensure a proper showing at a home World Cup, help change the perception of the game to the general public and lay down roots for long-term growth.

In some ways, Pochettino certainly succeeded. In others, he’s left the whole of American soccer wanting. It’s a fitting end for a coach who wanted so many people to believe – yet might never have felt that way himself.

#876. Rangers great Brand dies aged 89

Rangers say Ralph Brand will "forever be remembered as a great of the club"

Rangers have paid tribute to Ralph Brand, one of the most prolific goalscorers in the club's history, who has died aged 89.

A Hall of Fame forward at Ibrox, the former Scotland striker, who scored eight times in eight caps, netted 222 goals in 347 appearances for the Govan side.

Brand made his Rangers debut as a 17-year-old in 1954 and remained with the club until 1965.

He was part of four league-winning sides and won three Scottish Cups and four Scottish League Cups during his time at Ibrox.

After spells in England with Manchester City and Sunderland, Brand returned to Scotland to finish his playing career with Raith Rovers and Hamilton Academical.

"Ralph Brand's contribution to Rangers was vast and, through his Hall of Fame recognition, he will forever be remembered as a great of the club," the Ibrox club said in a statement.

#875. Familiarity of Doha drives home just how far Socceroos have come in recent years | Joey Lynch

There is increasing evidence of an evolution not only in approach but also mentality, highlighted by a return to the scene of Asian Cup heartbreak

Last week’s 3-0 dismissal of Qatar at the Abdullah bin Khalifa Stadium marked the first time the Socceroos had returned to the Gulf state since their heartbreaking elimination from the Asian Cup just under three years ago. Back then, coach Graham Arnold called Doha a “home away from home” after they relocated there during the Covid pandemic, and went so far as to suggest that they would have some form of advantage at the 2022 World Cup as a result.

Wandering around the city in 2026, memories rush back of Socceroos fans becoming eager participants in the takeover of the city’s souks during the World Cup. So too the feelings of sadness to see the birds still cooped up in small cages at the nearby bird market. It evokes recollections of trips on the red Metro line out to the Al Janoub Stadium in Al Wakrah, aided by the faded posters and stickers celebrating the 2022 tournament’s arrival that to this day can still be seen in shopfronts. There’s the excitement, for some, when a stray cat reminds you just how personable the local felines can be, as well as the sense of unease that remains whenever one pauses to reflect on how all this was built and the hands that did so.

But for all the familiarity and continuity for the Socceroos – five players who were there when Son Heung-min broke Australian hearts featured in Friday’s win – being back in Doha rams home just how much has changed for this team, and how well and truly into a new era we are.

Tony Popovic occupies the dugout these days, after the defeat to Korea arguably represented the beginning of the end of Arnold’s tenure by sparking a fatigue that would culminate in a downturn in results and his resignation later that year.

Nestory Irankunda, the rapidly emerging star of Popovic’s team who now has eight international goals to his name, was about to suffer a 4-0 defeat against the Central Coast Mariners nearly three years ago. Alessandro Circati was left out of the Socceroos squad to ensure he retained his place in the Parma side seeking to secure promotion to Serie A. Paul Okon-Engstler, Patrick Beach and Lucas Herrington were all yet to play senior football.

These players, who all started against Qatar, are emerging cornerstones of a new Socceroos setup that fielded the World Cup’s youngest side in North America, before flashing signs of further growth against Brazil in September. On Friday, this talented group bullied the two-time defending Asian champions on their own turf in the first-half, putting the game to bed before Popovic swung the changes and things got disjointed after half-time.

There is increasing evidence of an evolution not only in approach but also mentality. Of players bringing to the national team the lessons they’ve learned not just in the green and gold, but also in their experiences at bigger, more demanding clubs and leagues – in part because of the platform they’ve been offered by Popovic.

All of which could make it serendipitous if Tuesday’s game against Jordan, at the symbolic home of his predecessor, proves to be the end of the Popovic era.

Sign up for expert analysis from Jonathan Wilson as well as a rundown of Australians playing in the major leagues

The players aren’t going anywhere but with his contract situation still up in the air, it could well prove to be Popovic’s last game in charge of the Socceroos if he doesn’t agree to an extension. Given the postponement of January’s Asian Cup, there may not be the send-off he might have envisioned. Instead, a 12,000-seat stadium – unlikely to be very full – will host a hastily relocated friendly that’s entire raison d’être has vanished.

Remarkably, after sensitive discussions to relocate Tuesday’s game after player resistance to travelling to Amman, in line with DFAT advice, Doha could once again be pressed into action to serve as a historic backdrop for the Socceroos, just as a pandemic already saw it become the site of many a moment of distinction.

#874. Madrid-bound Gabriel posts farewell Man Utd message

JJ Gabriel scored a hat-trick on his last appearance for Manchester United in September before walking out on the club

JJ Gabriel has confirmed his exit from Manchester United with a farewell video message in which he says the club will "always be part of my story".

The 16-year-old forward, who has a verbal agreement to join Spanish giants Real Madrid, walked out on United in September.

He has subsequently been training on his own in Spain after relocating with his family.

The 50-second video montage, posted on social media, begins with Gabriel penning a letter to United, and includes some of his notable achievements, including coming on for his first-team debut during a pre-season friendly with Atletico Madrid in Stockholm in August, when he was just 15.

Gabriel then thanks United's coaches and staff, plus his team-mates as he "begins my next chapter".

He has not returned to United since scoring a hat-trick in a Uefa Youth League game with Sabah in September.

Although United still hold the teenager's registration until the end of the season, it does not prevent him moving to a club in the European Union as he now has an EU passport through his mother, who is of Cypriot heritage.

Speaking to Spanish newspaper Marca earlier this month, he said his "dream is to win the Ballon d'Or".

However, Gabriel has now broken his silence on his controversial decision to leave United, having won last season's Premier League Under-18 player of the year award, United's U18 player of the year award and been top scorer in a side that reached the FA Youth Cup final and Premier League U18 cup final.

"I arrived in 2020 as a 10-year-old boy with big dreams. Here, I grew as a player and a person, from scoring at Old Trafford to receiving the Jimmy Murphy [Under-18] award . You gave me moments I will always treasure.

"To every coach, every member of staff, to my team-mates and everyone who supported me; thank you for believing in me and helping me grow. As I begin my next chapter, Manchester United will always be part of my story.

#873. DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's important.

Doing nothing might be the ultimate brain hack. When you're bored, the brain goes into default mode network. It's not only healthy for you, but it may also shape the very essence of your identity.

You know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black? It seems like it's not doing anything. But it's not doing nothing. It's syncing your messages, updating apps and running other background processes.

Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?

Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.

It's going over your memories, shaping your sense of who you are, imagining possible futures, helping you understand other people and connecting ideas.

That's your brain's default mode network.

Scientists conducted brain-imaging experiments in the 1990s and early 2000s to find out which regions of the brain were active during demanding tasks, like solving a math problem or memory exercise.

But to measure that, they needed a so-called baseline. They needed to know the level of brain activity at rest and during demanding tasks.

So, between the tasks, they asked participants to relax, close their eyes, stare at a fixed point on a wall, or try not to think of anything at all.

And they measured the participants' brain activity both when they were solving a task and doing nothing. That's how scientists noticed the brain was active in up- and downtime.

They noticed that when participants started to focus on a new task, after having done nothing, some brain areas lit up and other areas dimmed down. That suggests those areas that dimmed down must have been active while the participant was apparently — physically and mentally — at rest.

This realization eventually led to the discovery of the default mode network or DMN.

The DMN is crucial because it helps your brain make sense of your life and experiences.

It helps you connect and revisit memories, reflect on who you are, imagine what might happen in future scenarios, understand other people, build meaning from experience, and connect ideas in new ways.

It turns all your memories, experiences, knowledge, emotions and social information into your internal story. Think of that story as a constantly evolving, updated model of who you are and how you engage with the world around you.

But it's important to understand the DMN involves more than one area of the brain. It is a group of brain regions that light up when you're not focused on an external task.

There's another player in your brain that acts as a monitoring system. You can think of it as constantly asking "Is there anything that needs my attention?"

Imagine you're daydreaming while driving, and a car suddenly swerves into your lane.

In a fraction of a second, your daydream disappears and your attention snaps back to the road. That player is called the salience network, or SN.

The salience network helps you notice important signals, like a sound, a mistake, pain, an emotion, a threat, or something happening in your body, and helps shift the brain toward attention and control systems when action is needed.

The DMN, SN and attention/control systems constantly interact.

And the DMN doesn't just turn off completely with every hard task. Parts of it can also contribute when tasks involve memory, stories, meaning or other people.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Smartphones have filled many of the small empty moments of our days — waiting for the bus, standing in line, eating alone, lying on the couch. We are constantly looking at our devices.

So, it seems reasonable to ask: are we crowding out those moments of boredom where DMN kicks in?

Maybe. But so far, there's no strong evidence that scrolling directly affects mental health by reducing DMN time.

What we do know is that problematic smartphone use can increase stress, anxiety, task-switching and disrupt sleep.

And sleep loss and stress also have clearer evidence for altering DMN-related brain connectivity.

When your mind wanders, it might produce a great new idea.

But it might also replay an embarrassing thing you did five years ago. Again. And again.

In depression, the self-reflection part of the DMN can get caught in repetitive negative loops that are hard to stop — what's known as rumination.

Scientists have also found that Alzheimer's disease targets key DMN areas, particularly those responsible for your autobiographical memory and remembering other aspects of the past. Which may help explain why memory problems are so central to the disease.

Protect your sleep and take stress seriously. There is direct evidence that sleep loss and stress disrupt DMN-related connectivity.

Take real, quiet breaks after mentally demanding tasks, like studying. It can even help you memorize facts for your exam.

Try to reframe boredom as this essential, energy-intensive active work in your brain that builds your internal narrative and sense of self, consolidates memories, creates connections and sparks creativity.

Try waiting in line without checking your phone. Look out the window next time you take the bus or take a walk without listening to anything.

You can also try scheduling DMN time. It may be the closest thing to a real brain hack.

#872. Rooney says he considered taking his own life at Man Utd

Rooney scored 53 goals in 120 appearances for England

Warning: This article contains references to suicide

Wayne Rooney says he was "contemplating suicide" during his playing days at Manchester United and was "speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up".

The former England captain joined United from Everton in 2004 and went on to become the club's record goalscorer, with 253 goals in 559 appearances.

But Rooney, speaking with Gabby Logan on the Life at the Midpoint podcast, external, detailed his struggles off the pitch when eldest son Kai, who is now 17, was a baby.

"When I was drinking, I would lock myself in my house for two days and just drink," said Rooney, when asked about the lowest point in his life.

"This is probably in my best part of my career playing wise."

The 41-year-old went on to explain how he "struggled to deal with it all" and, after opening up to his wife Coleen and his mother, knew he "needed help to get through it".

"I can look back and say I was selfish, but I knew I was going through something which I was really struggling to deal with," he added.

"I didn't want Kai seeing me like that, so that's why I'd hide away as well.

"I got to a place where you're contemplating suicide. I just didn't want to be around anyone. I didn't want to see people in the streets. I didn't want to go into shops.

"I was always comfortable on a football pitch, but everything else, [I] really struggled with it."

Rooney, who scored 53 goals in 120 England appearances, was recently named pundit of the year at the Broadcast Sport Awards and is currently appearing on reality TV show I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.

He helped United win five Premier League titles, the Champions League, Europa League, FA Cup and three EFL Cups before leaving them to return to the Toffees in 2017.

But the former forward said he learned to mask his feelings during his lowest moments.

"You don't want to show any weakness, so you try to mask it," Rooney added.

"Even though I knew the position I was in, it was difficult to actually admit that I was in that position because I felt like you feel less of a man, if you like, for doing that.

"I was speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up with me because when I look back I was probably at the height of my career, I've just had a young son, I've just been married.

"It should be the happiest point in my life and it wasn't.

"It was probably the lowest point because of the selfish acts I was taking.

"Coleen helped me massively. She could have walked away, it was that bad, but she stuck by me and helped me get through it."

If you have been affected by issues raised in this article, there is information and support available on BBC Action Line.

#871. A long wait, some magic and that smile: Ronaldinho savours Ravenna debut at 46

Brazilian legend, an investor at Serie C club, showed glimpses of old brilliance as he played 45 minutes for the promotion-chasing side

It may have been the longest buildup in world football. In June, the former Barcelona and Brazil legend Ronaldinho was unveiled by the Serie C side Ravenna to make his comeback at the age of 46 – 11 years after his last official game. Then silence.

But on a chilly November day on the eastern coast of Italy, there he was, not only in the squad, but in the starting XI for the eagerly anticipated derby against Forlì as Ravenna chase promotion.

The Ravenna manager, Andrea Mandorlini, deployed Ronaldinho in a central position, just behind the striker Simone Rabbi. The Brazilian held his position well, but was slow to get going. As the game progressed, he warmed up and showed his excellent skills; some things do not appear to change. Ronaldinho touched the ball 25 times, took three corners – one of which nearly led to a Ravenna goal – and initiated the move that led to the hosts taking the lead in the 35th minute.

Having trained with the team just once, whether he plays again remains to be seen. But he had already sprinkled some magic on a club and a region that has not made headlines in years. He played the first half as Ravenna won 2-0 to stay second in the division’s Group B (the Italian third tier is divided into three regional sections). Only the group winners earn promotion and Ravenna trail Spezia by six points.

Whatever happens for the remainder of the season this has put the club back on the football map. Ravenna’s highest finish was eighth in Serie B, in 1996-97, but this match was broadcast live by Sky Sports in Italy and shown in several other countries. It even appeared on the giant screens in New York’s Times Square, where the club’s owners, the Cipriani family, have built much of their international reputation through Harry’s Bar.

The town’s mayor, Alessandro Barattoni, who, as always, was watching the game from the stands, said: “A champion like Ronaldinho, a world football icon, brings great visibility and today is an opportunity for us to showcase Ravenna around the world, from our stadium. It is something new for us and together with the club the municipality will try to understand how this can have a positive impact on the town.”

The local community had been excited at the prospect of Ronaldinho representing the club, but there was some regret, too. “It would have been nice if he had come to take a stroll around the city, among the people who live here and own the shops,” the barista Barbara said before the game.

So how did he end up here? The Brazilian is a friend of Ignazio Cipriani, the owner of the Giallorossi. Lorenzo Tonetti and Ariedo Braida, old acquaintances from Ronaldinho’s time at Milan, are also part of the club. They convinced him to become an investor in the club and to pull on his boots again. In addition, Ravenna are now wearing his R10 sportswear line and one of the stands bears the same name.

Ravenna are aiming high. Cipriani has never hidden the fact he is aiming for Serie A, which is ambitious for a city with a population of 156,000. And Sunday brought hope, Dinho stepping on to the pitch in a gold-trimmed kit picked by the club to celebrate his arrival (and available for sale at €120). His hair was kept in check by a black headband and he was wearing gloves on a chilly afternoon. On his back, the No 10, something more than just a number for him, the man who became a global hero thanks to his extraordinary skill and contagious smile.

A younger generation has been able to discover Ronaldinho’s genius through the endless supply of online videos showcasing his greatest moments. Children who have never seen him play know his tricks and signature moves, while their parents can relive an era of football they may feel no longer exists.

“Dad, was he strong?” a young girl asked her father as they walked hand in hand towards the stadium. “Yes, he was strong. Actually, he is strong,” he corrected himself.

Our picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown in

One family had left Rome at 5am and travelled the 350km north just because their son had watched Ronaldinho on YouTube and wanted to see him live. Others had travelled even further, with supporters arriving from Turkey and Canada.

Ronaldinho hahas scored 299 professional goals, but his landmark 300th on his return was not to be. However, in front of a record attendance of 6,743 the way he initiated the move for Giulio Donati’s goal was ample reward for those who had turned up. Donati made his Serie A debut on 29 August 2010 for Lecce, at San Siro, against Milan, marking the Brazilian that day.

As Ronaldinho walked off at half-time, he was surrounded by a media scrum. After the game, he spoke of his desire to play again. “It all went by too quickly,” he said. “Football is like that, it’s always been like that for me.”

Who knows, perhaps he enjoyed himself so much that he wants to extend his career even further. “I don’t know, but if the president calls me, I’ll come back. It’s always a pleasure to play, I told him: ‘when he needs me, I’m there’.”

Mandorlini was effusive too. “We’re here and we’re truly proud to have been the architects of this match you played in,” he told the Brazilian. “So, if you want to play another one, that’s fine.”

Who knows what the future holds? For now, Ravenna fans will always have this: a day when a true legend connected people from around the world and allowed them, for one afternoon, to dream.
